data.text/markdown:
🛒 Rossmann Store Sales — EDA & Forecasting

Machine Learning coursework — sales forecasting for Rossmann drugstores. Data: train.csv (~1.02 M daily store records, 2013-01-01 → 2015-07-31) and store.csv (1,115 stores with static attributes), merged on Store. Scenario assumption: test.csv was not provided, so the last 6 weeks of the timeline (2015-06-20 → 2015-07-31) are held out as an out-of-time evaluation window. This mirrors deployment: train on the past, forecast the future, and avoids the leakage of random row-wise splits. Models compared
Model Notes
Naive baseline "last week, same weekday" sales per store (sanity check)
Ridge regression on log1p(Sales), one-hot categoricals, scaled numerics
RandomForest 300 trees, on log1p(Sales)
HistGradientBoosting sklearn gradient boosting, likely winner
Key design decisions (documented inline in the modules):
  • Modelling frame = open-store days only; closed days are trivially predicted as zero sales.
  • Customers is excluded as a feature — it is only known after the fact (leakage).
  • Lag/rolling features are computed per store on its open-day history and shifted by one open day, so the current day's sales never enter its own features. The assumed scenario is a daily one-step-ahead forecast.
  • Sales-scale lag features are log1p-transformed so a linear model on log1p(Sales) sees an approximately linear relationship.
  • All imputation statistics are fitted on the training split only.
1. Data loading & audit

data.text/html:
Shapes: train = 1,017,209 rows × 9 cols, store = 1,115 rows × 10 cols. Date range: 2013-01-01 → 2015-07-31. Unique stores: 1,115.

train.csv (first rows)

store.csv (first rows)

Missing values

train.csv is complete. store.csv has structural missingness: CompetitionDistance (3 stores), CompetitionOpenSinceMonth/Year (354), Promo2SinceWeek/Year (544 — exactly the stores with Promo2 == 0). These are handled with explicit flags + imputation in the pipeline.

data.text/markdown: 2. Exploratory data analysis

Observation: sales are stationary-ish around €270–300 m per month with a pronounced December spike (Christmas) and a visible dip in 2014 — consistent with the 2014 German recession and Rossmann's expansion lull. Strong monthly seasonality justifies the Month/WeekOfYear + sin/cos features.

Observation: Mondays are the strongest day (post-weekend + promo start); Sunday trading is rare (most stores closed) but the few open stores are busy. Promo days see roughly +40% mean sales. Both effects are strong model features (DayOfWeek, Promo).

Observation: store type and assortment separate store sizes — type d and extra assortment stores sell ~2× more than type c/basic stores. These are store-level (not day-level) features: they help the model learn which store is being forecast but they are constant per store.

Data quality audit

  • Closed days (Open == 0): 172,817 rows — all have Sales == 0 (deterministic; excluded from the modelling frame, predicted as 0).
  • Open days with zero sales: 54 rows — legitimate (e.g. refurbishment), kept in the frame; they inflate MAPE, so MAPE is reported with these rows excluded.
  • Stores missing CompetitionDistance: 3
  • Cross-check: Sales == 0 always coincides with Open == 0 or the refurbishment rows above — no inconsistencies.

Observation: raw Sales is right-skewed (long upper tail); log1p(Sales) is near-symmetric. Modelling in log space both stabilises the linear model and matches how percentage error (RMSPE, the competition metric) is measured. Predictions are inverted with expm1 before computing sales-scale metrics.

⚠️ Leakage guard: Customers correlates almost perfectly with Sales (r ≈ 0.95+), but customer counts are only known after the fact — they cannot be known for the day being forecast. Customers is therefore excluded from every model. (It would trivially "win" any leaderboard while being unusable in production.)

3. Feature engineering & temporal split

Implemented in features.py (see module docstrings for full rationale):
  • Calendar: year, month, day, week-of-year + sin/cos encodings of month and week; DayOfWeek.
  • Promotions: Promo, Promo2, Promo2Active (is the store's continuous promo active in this month and after its start date?), duration.
  • Competition: distance (+ explicit missing flag), months since the nearest competitor opened, open flag.
  • Autoregressive (leakage-safe): per-store sales lags (1, 7, 14, 28 open days), 7/28-day rolling means & 7-day std — all shifted by one open day so the row's own sales never enter its features. Plus days_since_last_open (captures the Sunday-closed → Monday pattern) and a HasLag1 flag.
  • Split: last 6 weeks of the timeline = holdout; everything before = training. Imputation statistics are fitted on the training split only.

Split summary

rows date range
Open-day frame 844,392 2013-01-01 → 2015-07-31
Training 804,110 → 2015-06-19
Holdout (6 weeks) 40,282 2015-06-20 → 2015-07-31
Features: 30 (27 numeric, 3 categorical). Closed days (172,817 rows) are predicted deterministically as €0 and excluded from model metrics.

4. Model comparison (out-of-time holdout)

Four candidates, all evaluated on the same 6-week holdout on the sales scale (predictions inverted with expm1):
  • Naive — same-store, same-weekday sales one week earlier (sales_lag7 before transform, with per-store median fallback). Any supervised model must beat this.
  • Ridge — linear model on log1p(Sales), one-hot categoricals, standardised numerics.
  • RandomForest — 300 trees, max depth 18.
  • HistGradientBoosting — sklearn's histogram GBM with early stopping.

data.text/html:
Results

🏆 Best model: RandomForest (log target) — holdout RMSPE 0.125 (≈ 12.5% typical percentage error), MAE ≈ €610 per store-day. Ranking (best → worst): RandomForest (log target) > HistGradientBoosting (log target) > Ridge (log target) > Naive (last week same weekday). Every supervised model crushes the naive baseline. The two tree ensembles land within a few tenths of a percentage point of each other, while the linear model trails as expected — the sales process is dominated by multiplicative interactions (store size × day-of-week × promo) that trees capture natively.

data.text/markdown: 5. Residual analysis, feature importance & submission

Observation: the 28-day rolling mean is by far the most important feature (it encodes each store's level), followed by the promo flag, day-of-week and recent lags — exactly the drivers seen in the EDA. Store type/assortment add modest store-level information on top of the rolling-mean baseline.

submission.csv

Written to the project root: 40,282 holdout predictions (open days only; closed days are deterministic €0 and would be added as PredictedSales = 0 in a real Kaggle submission). Columns: Store, Date, Sales, PredictedSales.

data.text/markdown:
6. Conclusions

  • RandomForest (log target) wins the out-of-time comparison: holdout RMSPE 0.125, MAE ≈ €610 per store-day — roughly a 3.9× error reduction vs the naive baseline.
  • What drives sales (per permutation importance): each store's 28-day sales level (sales_rollmean28), promo participation, day-of-week and recent lags; store type/assortment add store-level context.
  • Modelling in log space (log1p) aligns the linear model with the multiplicative nature of sales and the percentage-error metric.
  • Leakage controls: out-of-time split, no Customers, one-open-day shift on all autoregressive features, training-split-only imputation statistics.
Limitations & next steps
  • No test.csv was provided — the 6-week holdout is a proxy for the real forecast task; production deployment would need a rolling-origin evaluation.
  • Hyperparameters were fixed rather than tuned (a validation window inside the training period would be the next step); external signals (weather, regional holidays beyond the dataset) are absent.
  • The promo-effect estimate may still be optimistic for long-running promos ( Promo2 ) due to limited variety in the training window.
  • All artifacts live in artifacts/ (model_metrics.json, plots/); the holdout predictions are in submission.csv.
